name: Ethernet
basic: Frames carry local-link source and destination MAC addresses plus a payload type. A switch uses its forwarding table to deliver frames within the link domain.
intermediate: An endpoint sending off-subnet traffic normally addresses the local frame to a gateway, not to the distant server MAC.
advanced: VLAN tagging and MTU affect delivery. Link-up says little about IP configuration or application success.
example: Compare the endpoint link state and the selected next hop. Do not mistake a learned MAC entry for proof of permanent device identity.

name: ARP
basic: Address Resolution Protocol resolves an on-link IPv4 address to a link-layer address on networks such as Ethernet.
intermediate: A request asks who has the next-hop IPv4 address; a reply supplies the local delivery address. The mapping is cached.
advanced: ARP is not routed end to end and provides no built-in cryptographic proof of ownership. Neighbor-cache entries may be stale.
example: A request for a remote website usually requires the gateway mapping, not the remote server MAC. Inspect local cache context before interpreting missing entries.

name: IPv4
ports: IP protocol field, not a port
basic: IPv4 supplies 32-bit addressing and packet delivery across networks. A route selects the next hop for the destination.
intermediate: The header includes source, destination, time to live and payload protocol. TTL limits forwarding lifetime; it is not a wall-clock timeout.
advanced: Delivery can lose, duplicate or reorder packets. Fragmentation and path MTU require care; transport or application protocols supply additional behavior.
example: For the fictional 192.0.2.70/26 example, identify the containing subnet before deciding whether a gateway is needed.

name: IPv6
ports: Next Header field, not a port
basic: IPv6 uses 128-bit addresses and has no broadcast. A host can have multiple addresses with different scopes.
intermediate: Link-local communication and routed global communication have different contexts. Neighbor Discovery replaces the ARP role and also supports router discovery.
advanced: Routers do not fragment IPv6 packets; endpoints handle fragmentation when required. ICMPv6 feedback matters to path MTU operation.
example: Check both IPv4 and IPv6 paths when only some clients fail. Disabling all ICMPv6 can break normal network functions.

name: ICMP and ICMPv6
basic: Control messages report conditions such as unreachable destinations and support echo requests and replies.
intermediate: Echo success establishes a particular exchange, not that a web or mail service is healthy. Time-exceeded messages can support path investigation.
advanced: Filtering and rate limiting can hide responses. Some control messages are essential to ordinary protocol operation rather than optional diagnostics.
example: A browser can work when ping is blocked. A successful ping can coexist with a closed application port.

name: IPv6 Neighbor Discovery
basic: Neighbor Discovery helps IPv6 hosts discover local neighbors and routers and assess neighbor reachability.
intermediate: Neighbor Solicitation and Advertisement support address resolution; Router Advertisements convey router and link information.
advanced: SLAAC and DHCPv6 have distinct roles. The default router is learned through router discovery, not simply assumed from a DHCPv6 lease.
example: Separate neighbor reachability, address configuration and default-router selection when diagnosing IPv6.

name: TCP
basic: TCP provides an ordered byte stream between endpoints. The normal connection setup exchanges SYN, SYN-ACK and ACK.
intermediate: Sequence numbers, acknowledgments and retransmission support stream delivery. Applications must still define their own message boundaries.
advanced: Flow control protects receiver capacity; congestion control responds to network conditions. A stream can still fail and requires application error handling.
example: One send call need not equal one receive call. A connected socket does not prove the application accepted a request.

name: UDP
basic: UDP sends datagrams without a connection handshake or built-in delivery and ordering guarantees.
intermediate: Datagram boundaries are preserved at the API level, subject to receive-buffer handling. Applications decide how to detect loss or retry.
advanced: Applications can add reliability, congestion behavior and encryption above UDP; QUIC is an important example. UDP is not synonymous with insecure or always faster.
example: A missing reply cannot alone distinguish loss, filtering, a silent service or the wrong application request.

name: DNS
basic: The Domain Name System answers record queries. A and AAAA hold addresses; CNAME identifies an alias; MX describes mail routing.
intermediate: A client commonly asks a recursive resolver, which can use cached answers or contact authoritative infrastructure. Responses include status and time-to-live information.
advanced: TCP is part of ordinary DNS support, not only zone transfers. DNSSEC validation and encrypted DNS address different properties: authenticity versus transport privacy.
example: Distinguish NXDOMAIN, a record-type absence and SERVFAIL. A valid DNS answer does not prove the resulting application endpoint works.

name: DHCP for IPv4
basic: DHCP leases address configuration to clients. A typical initial acquisition uses Discover, Offer, Request and Acknowledge.
intermediate: A lease has a lifetime and can be renewed. Configuration may include a subnet mask, router and DNS information; relays can reach servers beyond the local segment.
advanced: Initial allocation and lease renewal are not identical exchanges. An offered configuration must be evaluated in the context of the intended network.
example: An address alone does not establish correct DNS or routing. Record the lease and options rather than guessing that every client shares one gateway.

name: HTTP and HTTPS
basic: HTTP defines requests and responses using methods, targets, headers and content. HTTPS applies protected transport to HTTP.
intermediate: HTTP/1.1 and HTTP/2 commonly use TCP; HTTP/3 uses QUIC. Cookies and tokens can maintain application context even though request semantics are stateless.
advanced: Caching, redirects and intermediary behavior affect what a client observes. Safe and idempotent method semantics do not guarantee an application is correctly implemented.
example: A 200 login page is not the requested report. Check response content, identity and side effects as well as status.

name: TLS
ports: Uses the service connection; not one universal port
basic: TLS protects application communication against eavesdropping and tampering when implemented and authenticated correctly.
intermediate: The handshake negotiates parameters and establishes keys. In a typical certificate-authenticated connection, the client validates the expected server identity.
advanced: Resumption and early data have different properties. TLS 1.3 early data can face replay concerns and is not suitable for arbitrary side-effecting operations.
example: Encryption without proper peer validation can connect securely to the wrong peer. TLS success does not establish application authorization.

name: QUIC and HTTP/3
ports: QUIC uses UDP; HTTP/3 commonly UDP 443
basic: QUIC builds secure transport on UDP. HTTP/3 maps HTTP exchanges onto QUIC rather than TCP.
intermediate: QUIC supports streams with independent delivery ordering and integrates TLS-based key establishment.
advanced: Loss affecting one stream need not block delivery on every other stream, although congestion and shared resources still matter. Connection migration depends on the protocol and deployment conditions.
example: Blocking UDP may prevent HTTP/3 even when HTTPS over TCP works. Observe the negotiated protocol rather than guessing from the URL.

name: SSH
basic: Secure Shell supports authenticated remote access over an encrypted transport.
intermediate: Server host-key verification and user authentication are separate steps. A host key identifies the server; a user credential identifies the account.
advanced: Sessions can carry channels such as terminal access, commands or file transfer. Authorization and forwarding policies determine what an authenticated user may do.
example: Investigate a host-key change through an independent trusted channel; do not erase the warning simply to make login proceed.

name: SFTP
basic: SFTP performs file operations over an SSH-protected connection. It is a different protocol from FTP and FTPS.
intermediate: The server account permissions still control which files may be accessed; encrypted transport does not grant extra filesystem rights.
advanced: Subsystem configuration, chroot arrangements and allowed operations can restrict access. A successful SSH login does not guarantee that file transfer is enabled.
example: Separate host-key verification, authentication, subsystem availability and file permissions when diagnosing transfer failure.

name: FTP and FTPS
ports: FTP control commonly TCP 21; data uses separate connections
basic: FTP separates control commands from data transfer. Unprotected FTP does not provide confidentiality for login or file contents.
intermediate: Active and passive transfer modes establish the data path differently. FTPS adds TLS to FTP; it is not SFTP.
advanced: Firewalls and NAT can allow the control connection but block the negotiated data connection. Explicit and implicit TLS configurations must match the client.
example: Logging in successfully does not prove directory listing or file transfer will work. Inspect the selected data mode and endpoint policy.

name: SMTP and submission
ports: Common TCP ports: relay 25, submission 587, implicit TLS submission 465
basic: SMTP transfers mail between systems; message submission connects a sender application to its outgoing mail service.
intermediate: Envelope sender and recipient commands are distinct from the visible message headers. Authentication and TLS depend on the service role and configuration.
advanced: Mail can pass through multiple systems. Transport encryption on one hop does not mean end-to-end message encryption.
example: A server accepting a message for delivery does not prove the recipient has received or read it. Follow queue or delivery evidence.

name: IMAP and POP3
ports: Typical TCP: IMAP 143/993 TLS; POP3 110/995 TLS
basic: IMAP supports server-side mailbox access and synchronization. POP3 provides a different mailbox retrieval model.
intermediate: Reading mail and sending mail are separate services. TLS may begin immediately on an implicit-TLS port or be negotiated where supported.
advanced: Client caching, message flags and retention policy affect what appears deleted or downloaded. Check service configuration rather than inferring security from a port alone.
example: Receiving mail can work while SMTP sending fails. Diagnose the corresponding protocol and account settings independently.

name: SMB
basic: SMB supports access to shared files and other resources. The server evaluates identity and permissions for the requested operation.
intermediate: Negotiated dialect and authentication context influence available features. Share permissions and underlying filesystem permissions both matter.
advanced: Signing protects integrity; encryption protects content confidentiality when negotiated and required appropriately. They are different controls.
example: A visible share name does not prove file-read access. Confirm the allowed operation using the intended test account.

name: NTP
basic: Network Time Protocol helps estimate clock offset and synchronize time with selected peers or servers.
intermediate: Request and response timestamps help estimate offset and delay. Path asymmetry and measurement noise affect accuracy.
advanced: Time quality and source trust matter to logs and authentication systems. Network Time Security adds protection where supported; ordinary NTP should not be assumed authenticated.
example: Compare time source, offset and synchronization state. Matching displayed minutes is not a precise clock-quality test.

name: SNMP
basic: Simple Network Management Protocol reads or changes managed values represented by object identifiers, depending on access policy.
intermediate: A manager queries an agent; notifications can report events. Version and security mode determine the relevant protection.
advanced: SNMPv3 supports authentication and privacy configurations, but its existence alone does not prove both are enabled. Restrict management operations to their intended identities and paths.
example: A missing object can mean an unsupported identifier or insufficient view permissions, not necessarily an offline agent.

name: OSPF
ports: Direct IP protocol 89; no TCP/UDP port
basic: Open Shortest Path First is an interior routing protocol that exchanges topology information within an administrative routing domain.
intermediate: Routers form appropriate neighbor relationships and compute paths from link-state information. Areas structure the routing domain.
advanced: Neighbor formation and route installation have different prerequisites. Authentication, area settings and interface configuration affect operation.
example: A ping between routers does not prove an OSPF adjacency or the intended route has formed.

name: BGP
basic: Border Gateway Protocol exchanges reachability information and applies routing policy between peers.
intermediate: A working transport session is only one stage. Routes can be received, filtered, selected or rejected according to policy.
advanced: Path attributes, policy and origin validation have distinct roles. RPKI origin validation does not prove every aspect of an advertised path is legitimate.
example: A peer session can be established while no useful routes are accepted. Review advertised and selected routes in the authorized configuration.
